checks.rule: Determined boundary plans based on measurements require measurements accurate to +/-10mm.
Measurements for a determined boundary must be taken horizontally rather than along a slope.
Measurements must be taken from at least two defined points on surrounding permanent physical features.
HM Land Registry prefers measurement references from both sides of the boundary where practicable.
Permanent features used as references should reasonably be expected to remain in position for at least 10 years.
Features subject to natural growth or decay are not acceptable as permanent measurement references.
Do not promote a measured boundary row when stated measurement accuracy is worse than +/-10mm.
Do not use slope distance as though it were horizontal boundary distance.
Do not promote a measurement-based boundary from only one undefined reference point.
Do not treat vegetation or decaying features as stable control points.
Keep measurement provenance separate from title-plan red edging or general-boundary interpretation.
Require measurement method and reference points to be recorded before parcel-height sampling is accepted.
Only National Grid coordinates are accepted for determined-boundary coordinate plans.
National Grid coordinates used for a determined boundary must have absolute accuracy of +/-300mm.
National Grid coordinates used for a determined boundary must have relative accuracy of +/-10mm.
Coordinates should be recorded as metric eastings followed by northings.
A suitably qualified professional normally certifies the coordinate accuracy.
A certificate specifying better absolute accuracy than +/-300mm is acceptable.
Reject non-National-Grid coordinates from exact-boundary promotion unless converted and provenance is explicit.
Do not merge absolute coordinate accuracy and relative point-to-point accuracy into one metric.
Do not accept coordinate precision text alone as evidence of survey accuracy.
Keep easting/northing order explicit to prevent coordinate transposition.
Require survey certification or equivalent authoritative provenance before exact-boundary coordinate use.
Do not infer centimetre-level parcel alignment from coordinates whose absolute accuracy gate is not documented.
A determined-boundary plan must clearly show the extent of the boundary to be determined.
The plan should identify start, end and turning points, preferably by lettered points.
The plan must contain enough surrounding detail to relate the boundary to the Ordnance Survey map.
The preferred determined-boundary plan scale is no smaller than 1:200.
The plan must describe the relationship between the boundary and physical features where they coincide.
Permanent ground markers may be used where surrounding permanent physical control is lacking.
Do not promote an exact-boundary row when start/end/turning points are ambiguous.
Do not use a plan without adequate surrounding physical context as an exact geospatial anchor.
Do not scale exact coordinates from an unstated-scale plan.
Reject temporary stakes or wooden hubs as permanent control markers.
Exclude superfluous or contradictory plan information from automated boundary extraction.
Do not accept plans carrying accuracy-disclaiming wording as determined-boundary evidence.
A title plan provides a graphic representation of the general extent of land in a registered title.
Title plans show general boundaries unless a boundary has been determined under section 60 of the Land Registration Act 2002.
Urban title plans are usually prepared at 1:1250 scale.
Rural title plans are usually prepared at 1:2500 scale.
Large rural title plans may use 1:5000 or 1:10000 scales.
HM Land Registry does not routinely survey land when deed plans and Ordnance Survey mapping are compatible.
Do not treat ordinary title-plan red edging as an exact legal boundary.
Do not derive sub-metre boundary accuracy from title-plan scale alone.
Require determined-boundary evidence before exact-line promotion.
Where title deeds and mapped detail conflict, keep the parcel boundary candidate unpromoted pending better evidence.
Keep title-plan scale and survey-derived measurement accuracy as separate fields.
Do not infer a survey occurred merely because a title plan exists.
Estate plans must clearly show scale and orientation and be drawn to the stated scale.
The preferred estate-plan scale is 1:500, with 1:1250 sometimes acceptable where detail remains clear.
Plans marked 'For Identification only' or 'Do not scale from this drawing' are not acceptable.
The plan must be based on an accurate survey plotted to the chosen scale.
Survey accuracy is specified as 0.3mm at map scale plus one part in one thousand of measured distance.
Survey control stations should support setting out and final as-built surveys on the datum used for the original survey.
Reject plans whose printed/PDF scale has been altered from the stated scale.
Do not accept disclaimer-marked plans for precision parcel extraction.
Require metric measurements when using PG41 survey-plan evidence.
Keep survey datum consistent between original, setting-out and as-built measurements.
Require sufficient detail outside the site boundary to relate the plan to registered-title mapping.
Do not promote intricate boundaries when the chosen scale cannot resolve them clearly.
The Environment Agency LIDAR Composite DTM covers about 99% of England at 1m spatial resolution.
The DTM is a terrain model with surface objects removed using algorithms and manual editing.
The 2022 composite is derived from Time Stamped archive and National LIDAR Programme surveys.
Where repeat surveys exist, the newest best-resolution data is used.
Bilinear interpolation is used where data is resampled before merging.
The 2022 composite includes source surveys from 6 June 2000 to 2 April 2022.
Metadata index catalogues identify which survey contributed at a given location.
Data is supplied as GeoTIFF rasters in 5km tiles aligned to the OS National Grid.
Elevation values are in metres and referenced to Ordnance Survey Newlyn.
The composite uses the OSTN15 transformation method.
Individual LIDAR surveys contributing to the composite have vertical accuracy of +/-15cm RMSE.
Require source-survey metadata for each parcel location before treating composite elevation as temporally specific.
The Environment Agency LIDAR Composite DSM covers about 99% of England at 1m spatial resolution.
The DSM includes terrain plus objects such as vehicles, buildings and vegetation.
The DSM uses last or only laser pulse returns.
The 2022 DSM composite combines Time Stamped archive and National LIDAR Programme surveys.
Where repeat surveys exist, the newest best-resolution data is used.
Bilinear interpolation is used where data is resampled before merging.
Do not use DSM elevation as bare-earth ground elevation.
Do not subtract DSM from parcel boundary elevation without confirming the intended surface semantics.
Keep buildings and vegetation as possible surface-object contamination in DSM-based samples.
Use DTM rather than DSM for ground-height difference unless the business metric explicitly requires surface height.
Require source-survey metadata when survey age can materially affect surface-object interpretation.
Do not infer a matching DTM/DSM acquisition unless metadata confirms it.
Environment Agency Time Stamped DTM is an archive of site-specific raster elevation surveys.
Site-specific LIDAR surveys have been carried out across England since 1998.
Available DTM resolutions vary among 25cm, 50cm, 1m and 2m.
The DTM is produced from last-return LIDAR with surface objects removed.
Data is supplied as GeoTIFF rasters in 5km zip files.
Elevation data is in metres and referenced to Ordnance Survey Newlyn.
Data is aligned to the OS Grid.
Time Stamped LIDAR vertical accuracy is +/-15cm RMSE.
The transformation used is specific to the time period of survey.
Require survey date and resolution to be recorded with each parcel elevation sample.
Do not combine time-stamped tiles from different transformations without explicit datum harmonisation.
Prefer the highest suitable resolution only after confirming its survey date and coverage for the parcel.
Environment Agency Time Stamped DSM is an archive of site-specific raster elevation surveys.
Available DSM resolutions vary among 25cm, 50cm, 1m and 2m.
DSM contains terrain plus objects such as vehicles, buildings and vegetation.
Data is supplied as GeoTIFF rasters in 5km zip files.
Elevation data is in metres and referenced to Ordnance Survey Newlyn.
Data is aligned to the OS Grid.
Time Stamped DSM vertical accuracy is +/-15cm RMSE.
The transformation used is specific to the time period of survey.
Coverage metadata identifies survey date, product resolution, transformation and geoidal model.
Require surface-object semantics to be explicit before comparing DSM and DTM elevations.
Do not infer survey contemporaneity from matching tile names alone.
Reject parcel-height promotion when time-stamped DSM metadata cannot identify survey date and transformation.
The Environment Agency point cloud contains highly accurate 3D x,y,z points and component attributes.
Time Stamped DSM and DTM raster products are derived from point-cloud data.
Point-cloud attributes can support bespoke products such as canopy-height or intensity rasters.
Environment Agency site-specific LIDAR surveys have been carried out since 1998.
Point-cloud availability goes back to 2006.
A matching point cloud may not exist for every historic surface-model product.
Point-cloud processing classifies returns into ground and surface-object classes.
Manual editing of the derived DTM means classified ground points may not exactly match the final DTM.
Point-cloud data is available in yearly 5km download zip files.
Downloaded point-cloud files use LAZ format aligned to the OS Grid.
Tile size depends on the spatial resolution of the data.
Coverage metadata records survey start/end dates and component information such as average point density.
OS Terrain 5 is a mid-resolution digital terrain model of Great Britain.
OS Terrain 5 has 5m post spacing.
OS Terrain 5 provides 5m interval contours.
OS Terrain 5 is produced from photogrammetry.
The product is updated every three months.
OS Terrain 5 is available as grid data.
Supported formats include ASCII DTM grid, ESRI Shapefile and GML.
OS describes typical accuracy as greater than 2m RMSE.
In ASCII grid data, each height value is the mean height across the whole 5m pixel.
ASCII grid z-values are represented at the pixel centre.
A 5km tile contains a 1000 by 1000 grid of 5m pixels.
Use OS Terrain 5 only as a lower-precision fallback where Environment Agency high-resolution LIDAR is unavailable or unsuitable.
OS Net base-station coordinate standard errors are generally better than 0.008m in plan.
OS Net base-station coordinate standard errors are generally better than 0.020m in height.
OSTN15 defines OSGB36 National Grid in conjunction with OS Net stations.
OS describes OSTN15 as effectively error-free when GNSS positional errors are excluded.
OSTN15 agreement with old triangulation network stations is about 0.1m RMS for Great Britain.
OSGM15 standard error in height for Great Britain is 0.008m, excluding GNSS heighting error.
Track GNSS positional error separately from OSTN15 transformation error.
Track OSGM15 geoid-model error separately from GNSS heighting error.
Do not treat legacy triangulation coordinates as centimetre-equivalent to modern OS Net positions.
Record horizontal CRS and vertical datum explicitly with every promoted elevation sample.
Require OSTN15/OSGM15 or an explicitly documented equivalent transformation for GNSS-to-OSGB36/ODN workflows.
Do not infer parcel height-difference precision from transformation accuracy alone; raster and boundary errors remain separate.
